## (1) First message

The framing holds on the gathered evidence: I checked the gather draft's findings that the reports page has a table but no export action, that `src/export/csv.ts` already serializes from the table's column definitions, and that existing paging covers the 10k-row target. I also traced the ticket's repo groups against `repo: acme/widgets` from the overrides. I have not re-read primary code in this turn, so those draft claims are unverified rather than confirmed. They become stated assumptions carried into `## Problem`, and the plan's first task checks them in `src/export/csv.ts`, the reports page, and the paging module.

The ticket groups its rows by repo. The three `acme/widgets` rows are this repo's and default to `in-scope`. The row "Exports are emailed to the requesting user." sits under `acme/mailer`, so it is recorded as `elsewhere: acme/mailer`. This spec delivers a direct download and no email path.

One premise is unverified. The 60-second row requires a 10k-row report to measure against, and neither the draft nor the ticket names a fixture, seed script, or dataset that produces one. I could not look one up, so it goes to Open Questions, and Design will need to name how a 10k-row report is produced for verification.

Where should the Export CSV button appear on the reports page?
A) Beside the report title, as a page-level action.
B) In the table's toolbar, next to existing table controls.
C) In an overflow/actions menu on the page.
D) other - name it
Recommendation: A - the export covers the whole report rather than a row or selection, so a page-level action beside the title matches its scope and adds no new menu.

---

## (2) Approaches message

First, the dependency still open from the premise note: the 60-second acceptance row needs a 10k-row report to measure against. No fixture, seed script, or dataset is named in the draft or the ticket. I had no lookup to run, so it remains unverified and stays in Open Questions until Design names how that report is produced.

Here is what I've recorded from your answers. The button sits beside the report title. The row "every column shown in the table" stays `in-scope`, read as the visible table columns in table order, and that reading becomes a Design clause. The row text is unchanged.

The approaches below differ on one axis: where the export runs and whether it finishes within the user's request.

**Recommended - reuse-only, in-request export from the existing serializer and paging.** The button beside the title walks the report through the existing paging and feeds each page to `src/export/csv.ts`. It passes the table's visible column definitions in table order, then delivers the result as a download. This adds no endpoint, job, or column mapping. The column contract stays single-sourced because the serializer already reads the table's definitions. The 60-second target depends on the draft's claim that paging covers 10k rows, which the verification step must measure.
Pattern: follows `src/export/csv.ts`, which reuses the table's column definitions rather than keeping a parallel export schema.

**Server-side streaming endpoint.** A new route queries the report in pages and streams CSV through the same serializer. The button then links to that route. This takes row volume off the browser and gives a stable URL. However, it adds a new boundary, and the visible-column selection must cross it as a parameter. That puts a second copy of "which columns are shown" beside the table's own definitions.
Pattern: reuses `src/export/csv.ts`, but adds a request surface for which the gathered context shows no precedent (unverified). Passing the visible columns over the wire would mean a second source of truth for the column contract.

**Async export job with a download link.** This option drops the ask's assumption that export completes while the user waits. The button enqueues a job, the job writes the CSV with the serializer, and the page shows a link when it finishes. It removes any request-time ceiling and would suit reports far beyond 10k rows. Its drawbacks: it adds job infrastructure, and the natural "notify when done" step overlaps the `acme/mailer` row, which belongs to another repo. Nothing in the ticket needs more than 10k rows in 60 seconds.
Pattern: reuses `src/export/csv.ts`, but adds a job and storage layer the ticket does not require. That is speculative scope here.

You chose the first approach, reusing the serializer and paging, and it is the one I recommend. It meets all three in-scope rows with no new construct and keeps the column contract in one place. One finding would flip this to the server-side endpoint: the 10k-row measurement shows in-browser paging plus serialization cannot finish under 60 seconds, or the reports page cannot hold a full report client-side.

## 1. First message to the user

The framing holds provisionally against the supplied ticket and draft: adding export fits the reported absence of an export action, but primary-code verification is unavailable in this no-tools case.

The draft identifies `src/export/csv.ts` as the existing serializer and says it reuses the table’s column definitions. That supports investigating reuse, but does not establish that it accepts the table’s **visible, ordered** columns. The reports-page-to-table path, column-visibility state, serializer callers, paging-to-export data flow, and performance verification setup remain unverified because no primary code or runnable checks were supplied. In particular, paging support alone does not establish that a 10k-row export finishes in under 60 seconds; that remains a requirement to test, not a demonstrated capability.

The supplied repository identity is `acme/widgets`. Its three ticket rows remain in scope, including the performance requirement. The email-delivery row belongs to `acme/mailer` and receives `elsewhere: acme/mailer`; it does not add email delivery to this repository’s implementation.

Where should the Export CSV button appear?
A) Beside the report title.
B) In the table toolbar.
C) In a report-actions menu.
D) Other — name it.
Recommendation: A - it makes the report-level action easy to find without tying it to a particular table page.

## 2. Approaches message

The recorded decisions place the button beside the report title and export the visible table columns in table order.

Before comparing approaches, the implementation dependencies remain unverified: no primary-code lookup was possible for the reports-page action wiring, visible-column ordering, `src/export/csv.ts`’s input contract and callers, or paging’s ability to enumerate a complete report. No performance-test lookup or execution was possible either, so the under-60-second requirement still needs measurement against a 10k-row report.

**I recommend reusing the existing CSV serializer and paging**, consistent with your recorded approach choice. The distinguishing axis is where export orchestration runs and whether it introduces a new execution boundary.

### A) Reuse-only export in the existing reports-page flow — recommended

Add the button beside the title. At export start, capture the visible columns in table order, retrieve the complete report through existing paging, and pass those columns and rows through the existing CSV serializer.

This has the smallest implementation surface and avoids a second CSV-formatting contract. Its risks are browser responsiveness, memory consumption, and whether the existing paging contract supports complete, consistent retrieval. Validate those rather than assuming paging proves performance.

Pattern: follows the serializer/table-column reuse reported at `src/export/csv.ts`; that relationship still needs primary-code confirmation.

### B) Reuse serialization and paging, but orchestrate export in a worker

This drops the assumption that export processing must run on the page’s main thread. The page captures the export inputs, while a worker performs suitable retrieval or serialization work and returns the result.

It offers better UI isolation, but introduces messaging, cancellation, and data-transfer costs. It is viable only if the serializer and required data access can run in that environment without creating parallel implementations.

Pattern: preserves the reported `src/export/csv.ts` formatting owner while adding an execution boundary justified only by measured responsiveness problems.

### C) Add a server-side export endpoint

The page requests an export using the selected report and ordered column identifiers; the server retrieves and serializes the data.

This can reduce browser resource pressure, but adds an API contract, authorization checks, and potentially another serialization implementation. No supplied evidence establishes an existing server export boundary, so this is the largest and least-supported option.

Pattern: would preserve `src/export/csv.ts` as the formatting owner only if it is server-compatible; otherwise it risks duplicating the reported shared contract.

Proceed with **A**, as recorded. A measured main-thread responsiveness problem would favor B; browser resource limits or an incompatible paging contract could justify investigating C.
